1) Xanthoma disseminatum — Most likely. Fits 7-year history of central diabetes insipidus plus numerous reddish-brown papules/nodules beginning on the eyelids, biopsy showing foamy histiocytes, Touton-type/multinucleated giant cells and inflammatory infiltrate, CD68+ and CD1a/S100 negative. XD classically causes mucocutaneous xanthomas and DI and matches the clinical–pathologic picture.

2) Disseminated juvenile xanthogranuloma (systemic JXG) — Possible. Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a non–Langerhans cell histiocytosis with similar histology (foamy histiocytes, giant cells), can be multifocal and rarely cause DI; patient age makes this less classic than infantile forms but disseminated JXG can present in older children/teens.

3) Erdheim–Chester disease (ECD) — Less likely but consider. ECD is a xanthogranulomatous CD68+/CD1a– disorder that can cause DI and cutaneous lesions; BRAF V600E negative and young age argue against it, and MRI pituitary was normal, but ECD often has characteristic symmetric long-bone changes that would help include/exclude it.

4) Cutaneous sarcoidosis — Possible alternative. Sarcoid can produce chronic skin lesions and DI (rare), and granulomatous inflammation with giant cells is seen; however the described xanthomatous (foamy) histiocytes and negative S-100/CD1a favor a histiocytosis over sarcoid.

5) Rosai–Dorfman disease / other non–Langerhans cell histiocytosis NOS — Less likely. Some overlap in presentation and histology exists; Rosai–Dorfman usually shows S100 positivity (often negative here), but other rare histiocytic disorders remain a remote possibility.

Recommended next steps to confirm diagnosis (for your clinician to order):
- Full lipid panel (to document lipid status; XD usually occurs with normolipidemia).
- Skeletal imaging of long bones (plain radiographs AP/lateral femur/tibia) — ECD shows symmetric osteosclerosis; XD/JXG typically do not.
- Chest radiograph or CT chest (evaluate for pulmonary/mediastinal involvement or sarcoidosis).
- Formal ophthalmology exam (slit-lamp and fundus) given eyelid involvement and risk of ocular disease.
- Consider additional immunostains (CD163, factor XIIIa) and repeat/second-opinion dermatopathology review to further classify the histiocytic lineage.
- If systemic disease is suspected after these tests, consider whole-body PET-CT and referral to hematology/oncology and dermatology experienced in histiocytoses.
